classification.difficultyReason: Translate line gradients into tangent ratios, apply the double-angle formula, and use the stated interval to justify division and select the angle.

inlines.text: Two distinct lines through the origin make angles
If the gradient of the second line is
times the gradient of the first line, find the angles of each line.

spec.sourceRegion: Left column, question 37, between introductory text and final instruction
spec.description: Arrowed coordinate axes and two arrowed straight lines through the origin, with two adjacent first-quadrant angle sectors labelled theta. No origin label, ticks, grid or numerical coordinates.
spec.mathematics: The first line makes angle theta with the positive x-axis; the second makes angle 2theta. Both sectors have equal angular size. Drawing coordinates describe illustrative geometry only and are not printed givens.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied question diagram remains visible; no numerical solution angles appear.

answer.short:
$\theta=\dfrac\pi6$, so $2\theta=\dfrac\pi3$.

Use $\tan2\theta=3\tan\theta$ and the tangent double-angle formula.
answer.worked:
The gradients are $\tan\theta$ and $\tan2\theta$, so
$$\begin{align*}\tan2\theta&=3\tan\theta\\\frac{2\tan\theta}{1-\tan^2\theta}&=3\tan\theta.\end{align*}$$
Since $0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{4}$, $\tan\theta>0$ and $1-\tan^2\theta>0$.
$$\begin{align*}2&=3(1-\tan^2\theta)\\3\tan^2\theta&=1\\\tan\theta&=\frac1{\sqrt3}\\\theta&=\frac\pi6\\2\theta&=\frac\pi3.\end{align*}$$
